summary.heading: The nuclear model of the atom
summary.html:
• Geiger–Marsden–Rutherford experiment: alpha particles (charge $+2e$) fired at thin gold foil in a vacuum; flashes on a zinc sulfide screen counted at different angles.
ObservationConclusion
Most go straight through or are deflected slightlyThe atom is mostly empty space
A few are deflected through large anglesThe positive charge is concentrated in a tiny nucleus
About 1 in 8000 bounce back (more than 90°)The nucleus also holds almost all the mass
  • The plum pudding model (positive charge spread out) can't turn an alpha particle round: its electric field is never strong enough.
  • The paths are smooth curves, because the electric repulsion grows gradually as the alpha particle gets closer. At SL only a qualitative description is needed.
  • Nucleus about $10^{-15}$ m across; atom about $10^{-10}$ m. The nucleus holds protons and neutrons (nucleons); electrons occupy the space around it.

summary.heading: Nuclear notation and isotopes
summary.html:
• A nuclide is written $^{A}_{Z}\text{X}$: $A$ = nucleon number (protons + neutrons), $Z$ = proton number (sets the element and the charge $+Ze$). Chemical symbols don't need to be remembered.
  • Number of neutrons $N = A - Z$. A neutral atom has $Z$ electrons.
  • Isotopes: same $Z$, different numbers of neutrons (different $A$). Same chemistry, different mass; some are radioactive.
  • Particles in the same notation: proton $^{1}_{1}\text{p}$, neutron $^{1}_{0}\text{n}$, electron $^{\;\,0}_{-1}\text{e}$, alpha $^{4}_{2}\alpha$.

summary.heading: Spectra and energy levels
summary.html:
• Continuous spectrum: all wavelengths (hot, dense object such as a filament). Emission line spectrum: bright lines on a dark background (hot, low-pressure gas). Absorption line spectrum: dark lines in a continuous spectrum (white light through a cool gas), at the same wavelengths as that gas's emission lines.
  • Only certain wavelengths appear, which is the evidence for discrete energy levels in atoms.
  • Emission: an electron drops to a lower level and one photon is emitted. Absorption: a photon is absorbed only if its energy exactly matches the gap between two levels.
$$E = hf = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$$
  • $E$ is the difference between the levels. A bigger drop gives a higher frequency and a shorter wavelength.
  • $1\ \text{eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ J. Levels are negative: zero is an electron that has just escaped. Ionization energy: the energy to free an electron from the ground state.
  • Absorption lines look dark because the absorbed energy is re-emitted in all directions, so less continues forwards.

summary.heading: The hydrogen spectrum and chemical composition
summary.html:
• Drops to $n = 1$: Lyman series (ultraviolet); to $n = 2$: Balmer series (visible); to $n = 3$: Paschen series (infrared).
  • From level $n$, the number of possible downward jumps (and so lines) is $\tfrac{1}{2}n(n-1)$: 6 from $n = 4$.
  • Cool hydrogen is transparent to visible light: the smallest jump from the ground state ($n = 1$ to $n = 2$, 10.2 eV) needs an ultraviolet photon (122 nm).
  • Each element has its own pattern of lines, so spectra identify elements in samples we can't touch: stars' atmospheres (E.5), flame tests and laboratory spectroscopy.
  • A whole pattern shifted to longer wavelengths means the source is moving away (Doppler effect, C.5).

summary.heading: Nuclear radius and density
summary.html:
$$R = R_0A^{1/3}$$
  • $R_0 = 1.20 \times 10^{-15}$ m (the Fermi radius). Eight times the nucleons gives only twice the radius.
  • Volume $\propto R^3 \propto A$ and mass $\approx Au$, so all nuclei have the same density: $\rho = \dfrac{3u}{4\pi R_0^3} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{17}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$ (as dense as a neutron star).
  • Nucleons are packed together like marbles in a bag, each taking up the same space.

summary.heading: Closest approach and deviations from Rutherford scattering
summary.html:
$$E_k = \frac{kq_\alpha Q}{d} \quad\Rightarrow\quad d = \frac{k(2e)(Ze)}{E_k}$$
  • Head-on collision: at the turning point all the kinetic energy has become electric potential energy (energy conservation; assume the nucleus doesn't recoil).
  • $d$ is an upper limit for the nuclear radius, not the radius itself.
  • At high energies the alpha particles reach the nucleus, the strong nuclear force acts too, and fewer scatter at large angles than Rutherford's formula predicts. The energy where this starts (set $d = R$) gives the nuclear size; it is lower for nuclei with smaller $Z$.
  • In exam questions energies are low, so only the electric force is considered.

summary.heading: The Bohr model of hydrogen
summary.html:
$$mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi} \qquad E = -\frac{13.6}{n^2}\ \text{eV}$$
  • Electron in a circular orbit held by the electric force. Bohr assumed its angular momentum is quantized; in the allowed orbits it doesn't radiate. $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ is the principal quantum number.
  • Combined with $\dfrac{ke^2}{r^2} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, this gives $r \propto n^2$ and the energy levels above (no derivation needed): $-13.6$, $-3.40$, $-1.51$ eV, matching the hydrogen spectrum.
  • Limits: works only for one-electron atoms and ions; can't explain line brightness; treats the electron as a particle on a definite path. Quantum mechanics replaced it but kept its energy levels.

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• "Most alpha particles bounced back": most went straight through.
  • Mixing up $A$ (all nucleons) and $Z$ (protons only).
  • Using one energy level instead of the difference between two.
  • Leaving energies in eV when $h$ is in J s.
  • Thinking an atom absorbs any photon with enough energy: for a jump between levels the energy must match exactly (only ionization accepts any energy above the ionization energy).
  • HL Using $A$ instead of $Z$ for the nuclear charge, forgetting to convert MeV to J, cubing instead of cube-rooting in $R = R_0A^{1/3}$, treating the closest approach as the radius, and dropping the minus sign in $E = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^2}$.

Evidence: Rutherford's shell-and-tissue-paper comparison: what exactly made the result so surprising, given the plum pudding model?
Only about 1 in 8000 alpha particles bounced back. How many counts would you need before you trusted such a rare result?
Models: What did the plum pudding model explain well? Why replace a model rather than adjust it?
List the atom models students have met (Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr). What new evidence forced each change?
Falsification: Classical physics predicted Rutherford's atom should collapse. Bohr simply assumed it didn't. Is that a scientific move?
Did the stability of real atoms falsify Rutherford's model, or classical electromagnetism, or neither?
Observations: Helium was named from a line in the Sun's spectrum before anyone found it on Earth. What does a spectral line actually let us claim?
Show a discharge tube through a hand spectroscope. What can students observe directly, and what do they have to infer?

oracy.html:
Odd one out (threes, 8 minutes): each group justifies one choice, then argues for a different one. Items: the nuclei of hydrogen-1, hydrogen-2, helium-3 and helium-4.

  • The odd one out is … because …
  • But you could also argue …
  • The other three all …

Listen for: correct use of proton number and nucleon number: hydrogen-1 is the only one with no neutron, helium-4 is the alpha particle, and isotopes share a proton number but differ in neutron number.

Can we know what we can't see?: Compare knowing the shape of an object in a sealed box by throwing marbles at it with knowing the nucleus from scattering. What makes the inference convincing?
Is a photograph through an electron microscope "seeing", or another kind of indirect evidence?
Is an old model wrong, or just limited?: Ask students for other models they still use knowing they are "wrong" (Newtonian mechanics, ray optics, the ideal gas).
Should exams ask for the Bohr model? What would be lost if it were dropped from the course?
How important are surprises?: Geiger and Marsden looked at large angles only because Rutherford asked them to check. What other discoveries came from checking something nobody expected to matter?
How can a research plan leave room for the unexpected?
Are pictures of the atom misleading?: Ask students to sketch an atom, then discuss which features of their sketch are physically meaningful and which are not.
Why do logos and textbooks keep the orbit picture? Is a familiar image worth the misconception it brings?
